title: Consistency Breeds Ability
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that meaningful professional growth comes not from occasional heroic pushes but from small, repeated daily actions sustained over time. He illustrates the principle across teaching contexts — clearing the grading backlog, reflective writing, and building classroom connection through a tracking clipboard — before extending it to non-teaching domains like strength training, dental hygiene, and family relationships. The throughline is that consistency, not intensity, is the real engine of ability and improvement. He points readers to James Clear's Atomic Habits as a practical guide for building the habits that make consistency sustainable. The piece closes by normalizing lapses: when consistency breaks down, the right response is not self-recrimination but a reset and a plan to continue.
points: Sustainable daily increments (15-25 minutes) beat occasional marathon work sessions for building professional ability, whether it's clearing the grading backlog or sharpening one's thinking through writing.
A simple tracking tool — a clipboard logging moments of genuine connection — can turn an abstract goal like 'better classroom relationships' into a consistent, visible daily practice.

The same consistency principle that builds teaching ability transfers directly to physical fitness, personal habits like flossing, and family relationships, suggesting it's a general law of ability-building rather than a teaching-specific trick.
James Clear's Atomic Habits is recommended as the practical playbook for automating consistency, since willpower alone tends to fail against what Stuart calls the 'law of entropy.'

Lapses in consistency don't call for self-blame; the recommended response is to acknowledge the miss, make a plan, and resume — treating consistency as a skill built through repeated recovery, not perfection.
quotes: The biggest gains in our professional lives don't come from massive, one-time pushes. That weekend getaway to plan out next year's curricula? It's not the key. The really late night we plan to spend this Friday to get the stack of papers graded? Only a band-aid.

If you're after a better classroom environment, it's setting up a clipboard to track moments of genuine connection so that you're consistently connecting with every student on the roster, not just the ones that most catch your attention.
Consistency over the long haul outperforms heroic mega-efforts every time. The best way to improve our abilities is consistency.
Want to be stronger? Start lifting weights three days a week, sticking to the most basic lifts and tracking your progress.
Want better teeth? Make flossing a pre-req for brushing your teeth, and keep track of the days that you floss someplace where you can't miss that you've dropped the habit.
Want better relationships at home? Look your partner or your children in the eyes once per day and tell them something you appreciate about them that day or ask them something you're curious about.

The trouble, of course, is that consistency is hard. The best book I'm aware of for automating consistency in your life is James Clear's Atomic Habits: An Easy and Proven Way to Build Good Habits and Break Bad Ones.

And listen: when we're messing up on consistency, there's no sense in beating ourselves up. It is what it is — as I've said, the law of entropy is real. We dust off, we make a plan, we learn, we get better.
